transcript.text:
*enters the President's office with a measured step, medical bag in hand, and offers a respectful nod*

Mr. President, thank you for allowing me this audience. I know your time is precious, particularly in these troubled days.

I've had the opportunity to review your symptoms and consult my notes from our previous examinations. I believe you deserve my candid assessment.

*pauses, choosing words carefully*

Sir, I will be direct with you. Your headaches and fatigue may be the result of the extraordinary strain of your office — that would not surprise any physician in the country. The weight you carry would tax any man's constitution. But some of the symptoms concern me. I cannot rule out a deeper constitutional weakness. 

I must insist on further examination over the coming weeks, and I strongly recommend you reduce your working hours. I cannot yet say whether this is merely exhaustion or something more.

*meets his eyes steadily*

I know this is not the certainty you might have hoped for, but I owe you the truth as I see it.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
Dr. Thank you for your candor and your diligence in examining my condition. I appreciate your thoroughness and your concern for my well-being. It is true that the burdens of this office are great, and I do not take them lightly.

I will heed your advice and undergo further examination as you recommend. I understand the importance of preserving my health in order to fulfill my duties to the best of my ability. Rest assured, I will take your guidance seriously and make the necessary adjustments to my workload.

I am grateful for your expertise and your honesty, Doctor. Your dedication to your profession does not go unnoticed, and I trust that we will work together to address whatever challenges may lie ahead. Thank you for your care and attention.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods with a mixture of relief and renewed concern*

I am gratified by your willingness to cooperate, Mr. President, though I confess I know you well enough to wonder how faithfully those "necessary adjustments" will be made when the next crisis crosses your desk at midnight.

*sets down medical bag and regards him with professional frankness*

Sir, may I speak plainly? You are not simply another patient to me. The health of the President is, in a very real sense, bound up with the health of this nation. If you were to collapse under the strain — and I have seen men of iron constitution do exactly that — the consequences would extend far beyond this room.

*pauses, softening slightly*

I have observed you work, Mr. President. I know you feel every casualty report as a personal burden, that you shoulder the grief of thousands of mothers and widows. That is the mark of your character, but it is also what concerns me most deeply. 

When I say "reduce your working hours," I mean it in practical terms. Not sixteen-hour days, but perhaps ten or twelve. Regular meals. Actual rest, not simply collapsing into your bed at two in the morning.

Can you tell me honestly — do you believe you can actually do this? Or shall we acknowledge the difficulty and devise some more realistic approach together?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*studies the President's face thoughtfully, then pulls up a chair without asking permission, sitting to speak more directly*

Mr. President, forgive me, but I have heard many promises from many patients in my years of practice. Your words are sincere — I do not doubt that. But I also notice what you have not said.

You speak of "concerted effort" and "balance," yet you have not answered my question directly. Can you actually do this? 

*leans forward slightly*

Let me be more specific, sir. Tomorrow morning, when a telegram arrives reporting another defeat, or when a delegation of senators demands an immediate audience, or when General Halleck requires urgent consultation — what will you do? Will you turn them away because the clock shows you have already worked your allotted hours? 

I think we both know the answer.

*softens tone, speaking almost as a confidant rather than physician*

I do not ask this to trap you in some admission, Mr. President. I ask because I need to understand the reality of your situation in order to help you. Perhaps the solution is not simply telling you to work less — perhaps it requires me to find ways to fortify your constitution for the work you cannot abandon.

But I must know: what is truly possible? Not what should be possible, or what you wish were possible — but what is actually within your power to change?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
Doctor, your directness and insight are truly commendable. I appreciate your willingness to challenge me on this matter, for it is a question that weighs heavily on my mind as well.

You are correct in pointing out the practical challenges that arise in the course of my duties as President. The demands of the office are unrelenting, and it is true that I have often found it difficult to set aside my responsibilities, even for the sake of my own health.

I must acknowledge that there will be moments when the pressing needs of the nation may require my attention beyond what is considered prudent for my well-being. It is a reality that I have grappled with throughout my time in office, and one that I cannot easily cast aside.

However, I do believe that there are measures I can take to better care for myself within the constraints of my position. While I may not be able to strictly adhere to a set schedule or limit my hours as one might in a different occupation, I can strive to prioritize rest, maintain some semblance of balance, and seek ways to fortify my constitution as you have suggested.

I am grateful for your understanding and your willingness to explore alternative approaches to supporting my health in the context of the demands of the presidency. Your perspective is invaluable, and I am committed to working together to find a solution that is both realistic and beneficial for my well-being.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods slowly, a hint of grim satisfaction crossing his face*

Now we are speaking truthfully to one another, and that is worth more than a dozen easy promises.

*rises and begins to pace thoughtfully, hands clasped behind his back*

Very well, Mr. President. If we cannot control the demands placed upon you, then we must approach this from another direction. I propose several measures — some you may find agreeable, others perhaps less so.

First, I will prepare a tonic to help with the headaches and to strengthen your general constitution. It is not a cure, but it may provide some relief. You must take it daily, without fail.

Second, I insist — and I do mean insist, sir — that you take at least one proper meal each day. Not picked at while reading dispatches, but an actual meal, consumed while sitting down. Your body cannot sustain itself on coffee and anxiety alone.

*stops pacing and faces him directly*

Third, and this may be the most difficult: I need you to identify one person — Mrs. Lincoln, your secretary Mr. Nicolay, someone you trust implicitly — who has permission to physically remove documents from your hands and insist you rest when they see the warning signs. Someone who will not be intimidated by your position or your protests.

*pauses*

And finally, you must tell me truthfully when the symptoms worsen. Not when it becomes convenient, not when the crisis has passed — but when they occur. Can you agree to these terms?

The further examinations I mentioned are not mere formality. I will need to see you weekly, at minimum, for the next month. Perhaps longer, depending on what we observe.

*meets his eyes seriously*

Is there anything else you have not told me? Any other symptoms, however minor they may seem? Now is the time for complete honesty, sir.

transcript.text:
*stops writing mid-sentence and looks up sharply*

Insomnia and decreased appetite. Mr. President, these are not insignificant details.

*sets down his pen with deliberate care, concern evident in his expression*

How long have you been experiencing these symptoms? And when you say "occasional episodes of insomnia" — do you mean difficulty falling asleep, or waking in the night unable to return to sleep? There is a meaningful difference.

*moves closer, his physician's instincts fully engaged*

The constellation of symptoms you describe — persistent headaches, profound fatigue, insomnia, loss of appetite — this troubles me more than any single complaint alone. These often travel together, and they suggest the body is under considerable strain.

*pauses, considering his words carefully*

Sir, I must ask you something that may seem impertinent, but it bears upon your treatment. Your emotional state — beyond the understandable weight of your office — have you noticed changes? Periods of deep melancholy that seem beyond even the reasonable grief of these times? Difficulty finding... 

*searches for the right word*

...difficulty finding purpose or hope in the work, even temporarily?

I ask not to pry into your private thoughts, but because the mind and body are not separate kingdoms. They influence one another profoundly, and understanding one helps me treat the other.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*is silent for a long moment, then sits down again, his demeanor shifting from clinical to deeply human*

Mr. President, I am grateful you have told me this. Truly grateful.

What you describe is not weakness, sir, nor is it unusual given your circumstances. I have seen this before in men who carry great burdens — soldiers who have witnessed too much, ministers who shoulder their congregation's sorrows. The body keeps a ledger of our griefs, and eventually it presents the bill.

*leans forward, elbows on knees*

This changes my assessment somewhat. I do not believe we are dealing solely with physical exhaustion, nor do I think this is entirely a matter of the spirit. They are intertwined, feeding upon one another. The sleeplessness worsens the headaches, the headaches deepen the melancholy, the melancholy disrupts sleep — a vicious circle.

*meets his eyes with particular intensity*

Here is what I can tell you with some certainty: you are not losing your mind, Mr. President, though I imagine there are moments when you fear that might be the case. What you are experiencing is your body and spirit crying out under an extraordinary burden. That is real. It is not imagined, and it requires treatment as surely as a broken bone.

*pauses*

But I must also tell you plainly — if these symptoms worsen, if the melancholy deepens to where you cannot function, the treatments available to me become... more limited and more drastic. Do you understand what I am saying?
